title: Of books
hook: he reads for pleasure and puts down any book that bores him (Essays 2.10)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fall from the horse. Your line was softer than feared. Did you catch a dread that turned out heavier than the thing itself? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-seven.

A bookmark that hasn't moved since spring. It's sitting in a book on the nightstand, a book you were told was important, and every night it gets a little heavier with guilt. Close by, maybe, there's another book you'd actually love to read, waiting its turn. Montaigne kept a library at the top of his tower. And in his essay Of Books, he tells us exactly what he does with the ones that bore him. He doesn't feel bad about it.
screen: `A BOOKMARK THAT HASN'T MOVED.` → `A LIBRARY IN A TOWER.` → `NO GUILT.`

segments.voice: First, why he reads. Montaigne says he looks for nothing in books except pleasure, honest amusement. Or, if he studies, he looks only for the learning that teaches him to know himself, and to live well and die well. That's his whole reading list: delight, or wisdom he can use. Second, no biting nails. When he hits something hard in a book, he says, he doesn't bite his nails over it. He gives it a charge or two, and if it won't open, he leaves it. Pushing harder only clouds his mind. And if a book bores him, he picks up another. Third, books in pieces. He says he's fond of Plutarch and Seneca, partly because their writing comes in separate pieces. You can start, stop, and come back, without a long commitment. And he confesses, a little daringly, that Cicero's long warm-ups, the definitions and divisions before the point, wear him out. He wants to get to the meat. Fourth, notes at the back. Montaigne's memory was bad, and he says so. So he got into the habit of writing a short verdict at the end of a book, so he wouldn't pick it up again later thinking it was new. That small habit matters. Reading for joy isn't careless reading. He wanted what he read to stay with him and change how he lived. On an ordinary Tuesday, read for joy might mean closing the book you're dragging through, and opening one that wakes you up.
screen: `PLEASURE, OR HOW TO LIVE.` · `A CHARGE OR TWO, THEN LEAVE IT.` · `BOOKS YOU CAN PICK UP AND PUT DOWN.` · `A VERDICT AT THE BACK.` · then, large: `READ FOR JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put down one dull book. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind the things you're reading, watching or listening to out of duty. A book, a series, a podcast, a pile of articles. Take one and ask Montaigne's two questions. Does it give me honest pleasure? Does it teach me how to live? If the answer to both is no, picture setting it back on the shelf, without guilt. Then let one thing come to mind that you'd read with real joy. The bell holds the time.
Of books. Montaigne reads for honest pleasure or for what teaches him to live and die well, and when a book bores him, he picks up another. Today's word.
Your line: read for joy. Today, read one page of something because you want to, and when you finish, jot one line about it, the way Montaigne did. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often borrow his rule for their own shelves: read for honest pleasure or for what helps you live, and feel free to set aside what does neither.
